newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Southern Albania votes in relative calm.
newsitem.headline: Southern Albania votes in relative calm.

text.p: Southern Albanians determined to oust President Sali Berisha in early elections voted in relative calm on Sunday belying months of violence that left the region in the sway of armed gangs.

The distant rattle of machine gun fire mingled with the music of clarinet and tambourine bands outside polling centres. The bands became traditional during the single-party elections of the hardline communist regime that ruled Albania for 45 years until 1990.

Southern Albania was the starting point for the upheaval, in which more than 1,500 people have died and was sparked by the failure of five fraudulent investment schemes. Southerners say Berisha is to blame for allowing the schemes to flourish.

"Nobody wants Berisha here. He ruined a lot of people and he's not democratic," said Kosta Koco, an engineer waiting patiently in line with his family to cast his vote in the Adriatic port of Sarande.
"We don't mind his party but the man himself and nobody will vote for them."
Polls closed on time at 6 p.m. in most places, but one Sarande polling station remained open past the deadline to enable a crowd of latecomers to vote.

The depth of anti-Berisha feeling was demonstrated by a result officially declared within minutes at an old people's home in Gjirokaster, 40 km (25 miles) north of Sarande. Twenty-seven of 28 residents voted for the Socialist Party.
Berisha is not up for re-election but the poll is widely viewed as judgment on his five years in office. He has hinted he may step down if the Socialists score a big victory.
Observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), in charge of monitoring the vote, said voting appeared to go smoothly in the south.
Some voters were turned back when their names failed to appear on the registry.
"So far, so good," local election committee official Kosta Shendis said during the day. "We are new at this democratic procedure but I hope that everything will go well."
Officials from the OSCE say communications with remote villages are likely the biggest problem they will face.
In nearby villages dominated by Albania's Greek ethnic minority, voters began trickling into polling stations after the tolling of church bells signalled the end of Sunday's Orthodox service.
"We don't foresee any problems here. We're a small village and we all know each other," said election official Odise Dashi in the village of Cuka.

Armed youths who have been roaming the south and terrorising residents kept out of sight during the morning. Romanian and Italian soldiers from the multi-national force helping guard polling stations drove armoured cars through streets, escorting the OSCE monitors.
But residents were concerned about possible trouble during the vote count later in the evening, when observers must return to their bases.
"Let's hope the evening is as calm as the morning," an elderly Sarande resident said.
There are no members of the multi-national force in town and monitors must be escorted back to their base in Gjirokaster before nightfall.
